technique.how: Ask specifically about pain or burning on passing urine, new increase in frequency or urgency, and their onset; then ask about vaginal discharge or irritation, hematuria, flank pain and fever. Establish whether the symptoms are new relative to baseline (important in elderly or catheterized patients).
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to give a reliable history; in delirium, obtain collateral history of new urinary symptoms.

interpretation.positive_finding: In women, dysuria (LR+ 1.5) or frequency (LR+ 1.8) each raise UTI probability slightly; dysuria and frequency together without vaginal discharge or irritation raise it strongly (LR 24.6, probability above 90%).
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of dysuria lowers the probability only modestly (LR- 0.5); history alone cannot rule out UTI once one symptom is present.
interpretation.pitfalls: Vaginitis, urethritis and STIs mimic dysuria (vaginal discharge/irritation LR 0.2-0.3 for UTI). In elderly patients asymptomatic bacteriuria is common, and confusion without new genitourinary symptoms should not be attributed to UTI.
interpretation.changes_what: Dysuria plus frequency without vaginal symptoms can justify empirical treatment in women; absent or nonspecific symptoms should push toward other causes of fever, AKI or delirium.

estimates.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - finding: dysuria present
estimates.population: Women presenting with one or more symptoms of acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (9 studies)
estimates.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
estimates.quote: dysuria (summary positive likelihood ratio [LR], 1.5; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.2-2.0)

estimates.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - finding: dysuria absent
estimates.population: Women presenting with one or more symptoms of acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (9 studies)
estimates.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
estimates.quote: absence of dysuria (summary negative LR, 0.5; 95% CI, 0.3-0.7)

estimates.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - finding: frequency present
estimates.population: Women presenting with one or more symptoms of acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (9 studies)
estimates.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies

estimates.target_condition: Acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection - combination: dysuria and frequency without vaginal discharge or irritation
estimates.population: Women with UTI symptoms in the single included study that examined symptom combinations
estimates.reference_standard: Urine culture as defined in included studies
estimates.quote: 24.6 for the combination of dysuria and frequency but no vaginal discharge or irritation

sources.citation: Bent S, Nallamothu BK, Simel DL, Fihn SD, Saint S. Does this woman have an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection? JAMA. 2002;287(20):2701-2710.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: The LRs apply to non-pregnant women with uncomplicated UTI; do not apply them to men, catheterized patients, or elderly patients with delirium and no new urinary symptoms.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Urinary symptoms with fever, rigors, flank pain, hypotension or AKI indicate pyelonephritis/urosepsis, which needs cultures, antibiotics and assessment for obstruction.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Precision of symptom history is not reported in the abstract; symptom definitions varied across the nine included studies.

extraction_notes: All numbers from the Bent 2002 RCE abstract (PMID 12020306); JAMA full text and tables are not accessible. The LR 24.6 for dysuria+frequency without vaginal discharge/irritation comes from a single study within the review and has no CI in the abstract. No quantitative evidence was found for dysuria/frequency in elderly or delirious patients; the seeded 'elderly' tag and delirium differential are retained but the estimates do not cover them.
